title: Why you should leave reps in the tank (Reps in Reserve)
summary: Explains his strategy of always leaving reps in reserve on strength work: stopping short of grindy reps keeps form perfect, protects joints, preserves energy for the volume work that drives hypertrophy, and nearly eliminates injury risk. He contrasts the Western grind-to-failure mentality with the Eastern school's habit of repeating a weight until it's easy, and argues that slow, injury-free progress wins in the long run.

claims.claim: Leaving reps in the tank means if he could grind 6 reps on squats, he stops at 4 to get quality reps with perfect form and muscle activation without taxing the joints.
Leaving reps in reserve doesn't prevent progress: there is no absolute difference between getting your reps now or later, because you have time and aren't rushing a PR (unless you're a powerlifter).
The lifter who always maxes out reps may pull ahead at first, but the one leaving reps in the tank still adds a rep each time while staying fresh.
Nothing drains you more, mentally or physically, than grindy reps; strength work is always tiring but grinding takes far more out of you.

Opening a high-volume pull day with a grindy or failed one-rep-max deadlift makes the rest of the workout go badly: light weights feel heavy and you keep failing, because you programmed a day of failure.
He never wants to fail; he hits his strength PR knowing he could have pushed more, then enters the volume phase 'like a winner' and sets volume PRs.
For a bodybuilder the volume work is what matters; grinding the strength work keeps you from reaching the top of volume rep ranges (6-10, 8-12, 10-15).
Over a whole workout, the lifter who leaves reps in reserve moves more total weight because sub-maximal volume reps add up to more tonnage.
For hypertrophy, as long as you stay within the right intensity window, whether you work at 98% or 76% doesn't matter; total tonnage is what matters.
Very high intensity can help push the weights you use on volume days, but in his programs it isn't necessary.
He never does one-rep maxes or RPE 10 sets.
Staying within the rep range, avoiding grindy maxes and not taking sets to the last rep makes injury chances almost zero; chasing the last rep every time greatly raises injury risk.
The Western 'grind the last rep, work through failure' mentality produces injuries; the great athletes it produces were mostly gifted and would have succeeded on any program.
The Eastern school of weightlifting's mentality is much better and is gaining ground in the lifting community.
Eastern-style progression: if a weight is challenging for 4 reps, keep doing 4 reps with it until it's easy, then make a big jump.

A bodybuilder who doesn't care about strength can stay at the same 4-rep strength weight for one or two months while raising the volume underneath; you still move more weight overall and stay injury-free.
Strength work should prime you for the rest of the session, not tire you out.
Thinking in five-year horizons is pointless; you're in it for the long run, and if the fast guy stalls after two years, reaching his level in five means you then pass him.
The lifter who grinds every rep often drops out from injury; bide your time, stay injury-free and put the work in.
He always leaves at least one rep in the tank.
